title: The Desire for Righteousness and the Praise of God
english: But facing the sun. Thus it is also said in Job: 'the stars are not pure before him'. Therefore, this 'according to your righteousness' does not at all mean: not according to your unapproachable righteousness, but according to your righteousness, in which you judge human things. Do not judge me according to their enmity, but according to your righteousness; for your righteousness hates the unrighteous.

25 Let them not say in their hearts, 'Well done, well done to our soul.' Even if they do not say it with words, let them not even say to our soul in their hearts, 'Well done, well done.' 25 Let them not say, 'We have overcome him.' Let them not say that we have surrounded him and conquered him; for often this too has been made clear, that according to the Scripture, downfall signifies victory.

26 May those rejoicing in my evils be shamed and put to shame. It brings salvation to those being shamed and being put to shame because of what they are doing badly; for since they want to surround me with evils and rejoice having seen what they strive to complete, let them be shamed; for having been shamed, they will no longer lie in wait for me, having been put to shame, they will no longer do these things bearing mockery and accusation. Moreover: he says 'evil things', not 'wickednesses'? For he who says, 'Judge me, Lord, according to your righteousness,' truly had no wickednesses; he who says, 'those rejoicing in me unjustly.'

26 Let those boasting against me be clothed in shame and confusion. The great ones speaking against me arrogantly and rejoicing, may they be shamed and put to shame, and may they know themselves. But this happens as a call to them, and I no longer have them lying in wait like that. Previously he prays for them, but secondly also for himself. Moreover: the 'to clothe oneself'? As we say to clothe oneself in a virtue, or to clothe oneself in a wickedness, or to clothe oneself in a 'garment of salvation': 'Let my soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a robe of gladness' (Psalm 31:11). The quality becomes like a garment of the thing.

27 May those desiring my righteousness rejoice and be glad. 230 When 'those boasting' are said to 'clothe themselves in confusion and shame', 'those desiring my righteousness and my peace' rejoice and are glad. When the enemies are shamed and put to shame, the friends rejoice and are glad.

They are those who desire my salvation, my virtue, and my righteousness. And let them say continually, 'Magnified be the Lord.' Then they magnify the Lord continually, when I remain continually in righteousness, in not falling to the evil ones.

They are those who desire the peace of his servant—me, his servant. 'Let them say continually, Magnified be the Lord,' seeing me making peace, seeing me not having fallen to trouble or confusion or uprising or war. We have said many times that sometimes the whole is shown through the individual parts, and we used to employ this witness by saying: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent of hands' (Ps 24:3). Then he says: 'This one shall receive a blessing from the Lord.' He does not say something explicit, but if anyone is such a person, if anyone has ascended the mountain and stood upon the mountain of the Lord and is innocent of hands, everyone, if anyone is such a person, 'shall receive a blessing from the Lord.' Similarly in Psalm 119, it is said: 'The law of the Lord is perfect, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful' (Ps 119:29, 138). And he says many things: 'For indeed your servant keeps them' (Ps 119:138). He does not say only himself, but if anyone is such a servant of God.

Being therefore inferior, when he speaks of achievements, he says 'to the servants of God,' but when of failings, 'to himself.' Some say that those approaching God are sons of God, but those who have reached them are these servants; for from servants they become friends and sons. The greater, then, are 'those who desire,' those who are like sons, those 'perfect as their father' who is the 'perfect one in heaven'; they desire to be the peace of also those who are lower. Or thus, that all desire the peace of each individual servant.

And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, all the day your praise. It shall meditate thankfully. When that which I requested exists, my tongue meditates on your righteousness. This I always recount, in hymns I bring it forth, in narrative words I name it. 'Day' here he says, the whole time of human life, just as in others he says: 'Because of you we are being killed all the day' (Rom 8:36), that is, because of strife. And the praise of God he does not say 'lordly'; rather, it is called a hymn and a song upon God, but upon men...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nobility of God's Servitude
english: Praise. It would be rightly called the praise of God and his praise. And 'praise of God' is possible, which he himself gives; for he himself praises those worthy of it. He says: 'and then praise shall be given to each from God' (Ps 18:9).

1–2 To the end; to the servant of the Lord, David. He says that the lawless one sins in himself. Much has been said about the end, that it is that end for the sake of which all other things happen, but it is not for the sake of anything else, which is called the last desirable thing. We desire certain things for the sake of something else. None of those is the end, but they are makers of the end. But the end is that which does not happen for the sake of something else, but for its own sake all other things happen.

Someone wants to learn grammar; he learns, he meditates, he listens to a teacher, and none of these is the end. But the very attainment of perfect knowledge is the end. Therefore, perfect virtue is the last desirable thing, with which there is no other thing to seek as a completion. We use laws for the sake of virtue; the giving of the laws is not the end. We are persuaded by exhortations, by teachings approaching moral training; but all these things happen for the sake of something else. But perfect virtue, the unsurpassed, established after all progress, is the end. Every servant of God pursues this end. Because of this: 'to the servant of the Lord, David'.

If it says 'to the servant', it is not only the end of this David, the son of Jesse, but of every one who has served God. If, indeed, we praise someone in grammar and say that he is able to write as is necessary, and to read as is fitting, and to explain as it is, the harmonies, we do not speak only about him, but about every grammarian. However, let us look at his service, so that we may thus see the others, the fellow-servants.

'I have found', he says, 'David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will' (Acts 13:22). The virtues according to species are the wills of God. But the general one is called one will; for he says: 'Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter, but he who does the will of my Father' (Matt 7:21). Here he named the general virtue as a singular will. And he performs the virtues according to species by doing all the wills of God, if anyone is a doer of the wills of God, if he...

If one turns his commandments into works, and if he does not cast away the things that are to be thought, then the truth of God has been shown. This one is a servant of God. And behold, he was a king saying these things, and he preferred the servitude of God to kingship; for to be a servant of God is a great nobility.

Indeed, it has been said many times that the saints position themselves in their prefaces thus: 'James, a servant of the Lord God Jesus Christ' (James 1:1), and 'Paul, a servant of Christ', and Jonah being asked, 'From what country and what people?', then he says, 'I am a servant of God' (Jonah 1:9). And just as those who are being promoted by virtue of their ranks claim their rank and dignity, these saints, as if professing a greatest nobility and surpassing fame and great rank, profess the servitude of God. The servant of God, knowing the will of God, knows also the things that are contrary to the will of God. For impiety, lawlessness, and every kind of evil oppose the will of God.

Therefore, the servant of the Lord, having known the end, which is virtue over all things, also knew lawlessness; for of the contrary things, there is the same knowledge. He who possesses medical skill knows not only the healthful things among the remedies, but also the harmful ones, so that he may use the former and reject the latter. Thus the servant of the Lord, being lifted up toward the end, says in the song: 'The lawless one says that he sins in himself' (Psalm 19:13).

The wording is ambiguous. It signifies one thing thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'. 'He says in himself that he sins'. First, he joins himself to lawlessness and sin, and thus comes to practicing it. It is impossible not to sin if one has not been pre-disposed toward sin. Thus 'he says' 'the lawless one that he sins in himself'. 'He says in himself'. For it is to be read thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'. But it is also possible to take the other part of the ambiguity thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'; for he knows that he has no boldness regarding sinning. Everyone who sins while following it hides the evil; for no one indeed makes himself manifest as he is. Even if he were a fornicator and wished to lie with someone, he does not want the one describing him to say he is a fornicator. Therefore, they are even more condemned, because they wish to hide what they are doing. No one...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Distinction between Lawlessness and Transgression
english: But one who does good wants to be unknown—and sometimes does this because of blindness—but he strives to have such works as being illuminated in addition to men, so that the Father who is in the heavens might be glorified; for 'let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in the heavens' (Matt 5:16).

2 There is no fear of God in the face of his eyes. No one having the divine fear before his eyes sins; for the divine fear is a refuter of sin. When [men] despise [it], sinning occurs, having become outside of the divine fear. In the same way also the divine writing of the proverbs introduces wisdom, saying: 'The fear of the Lord hates injustice, and insolence and pride and the ways of the wicked' (Prov 8:13). If the fear of God hates these things, no one having it acts unjustly; for 'the fear of the Lord hates injustice.' He is not an insolent man, he is not a slanderer, he is not self-willed. And the name of insolence (hybris) at times signifies slander, and at other times exaltation and arrogance. 'And the ways of the wicked the fear of God hates.' And the 'ways of the wicked' are the ungodly opinions and the lawless actions. Since, therefore, he does not have the fear of God before his eyes, because of this he says in himself that he sins. 'But from the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil' (Prov 16:6).

3 Because he acted deceitfully in his own presence to find his own lawlessness and to hate it. In his own presence he acted deceitfully. He hides the evil through deceit, knowing that, if he does not hide the lawlessness through deceit, once found, hatred is activated in the one who has found and known it. So that he might not be hated because of the lawlessness, he hides it through deceit; for the one finding it hates it.

232 You know that many times probabilities overshadow evil works, so that they may go unnoticed. For example, the false prophets, being 'snaring wolves' according to the opinion, bring a sheep's fleece, so that they may be thought sheep. And from which they want to be known as sheep, it is evident that they hate the wolf-like way; but they hide it; for if it is found, hatred is activated. And no one is so dishonest as to say: 'I love lawlessness and I hate piety'—for possessing it and finding pleasure in practicing it, he does not want to hate it—for if it were made manifest, he would be shown...

For it also brings punishment. The words of his mouth are lawlessness and deceit. The words which he brings forth are lawlessness and deceits. If he sins morally by being uncontrolled, angry, or unjust, his words possess lawlessness. If he deceives with false opinion, those words possess deceit; for he acts deceitfully so that the impiety of his words may not appear, lest they be trampled upon and some turn away from them.

Furthermore: did he not say 'transgression'? Transgression is lawlessness, but lawlessness is not always transgression. If one acts outside of the law, he is acting outside of it, and that is lawlessness. But if, having received the law, he violates it, he acts contrary to the law, and that is transgression. Therefore, transgression is lawlessness, but lawlessness is not always transgression. The one acting contrary to the law and acting in opposition to the law is judged by the extent to which it reaches into actual deeds. If, however, we see the disposition of the one acting, even one who has received the law but does not act according to it, he transgresses. But if he has no law, I say—as it is written—he only commits lawlessness. 'As many as sinned in the law' (Psalm 78:52), he says; those sinning in the law are transgressors. 'They sin lawlessly' are those not possessing the law. However, the thing being done is one and the same. I take the difference from the volition and the disposition of the one acting, so that at times he is called lawless, and at times he is called a transgressor.

He did not will to understand the good. Lest anyone think that it is nature which separates the servant of God from transgression, and the diligent from the wicked, [but rather] that he has assigned both to volition, and says that according to his own will he is either evil or diligent; 'he did not will.' But another wills to understand the good. The diligent man wills this very thing, to do good things. Again, he who is not in these things will have become outside of them by his own will. Thus the word constructs self-determination and that which is autonomous and free through volition, because no one is a transgressor by nature, and no one is good by essence; for we all humans are of the same substance. But according to our own choice, or flight, we are either wicked or diligent.
He reckoned lawlessness upon his own bed. He says this to mean that not only when he is awake and acting does he work lawlessness, but also upon the bed.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
